think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 9-year-old boy in rural Tanzania presents with a 1-year history of progressive, painful left scrotal enlargement and an irreducible cystic mass thought to be a hydrocele, but with negative urine and stool microscopy. Intraoperatively, the presence of thickened tunica albuginea and firm nodular lesions on an atrophic testis raised acute suspicion of testicular neoplasia, leading to orchidectomy. The tension lies in distinguishing chronic helminthic granulomatous inflammation from pediatric testicular malignancy in the absence of classic urinary symptoms (hematuria).
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission evaluation concludes after the physical examination, triage hemoglobin (11.5 g/dL), and negative baseline urine and stool microscopic examinations. Surgical exploration (hydrocelectomy converted to orchidectomy) and histopathology represent the invasive confirmatory phase.
3. Differential Distinctions: Idiopathic or communicating hydrocele presents with irreducible cystic transilluminating scrotal mass, but fails to explain testicular nodularity, tunical thickening, and underlying testicular atrophy. Pediatric testicular tumors (e.g., yolk sac tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma) present with firm testicular masses and nodularity, but histopathology shows no neoplastic proliferation, demonstrating instead characteristic granulomatous inflammation surrounding terminal-spined trematode ova.
case_prompt: A 9-year-old boy was referred to a regional medical center in Tanzania with a 1-year history of progressive left scrotal swelling accompanied by pain. The swelling had been gradually increasing in size. He had no history of fever, weight loss, night sweats, or gross hematuria. Prior treatment with traditional remedies, as well as oral courses of antibiotics and analgesics administered at a district hospital, had failed to relieve his symptoms. On physical examination, the child was well-nourished without pallor or jaundice. Systemic examination was normal. Local genital examination revealed a left scrotal mass that was slightly tender, cystic in consistency, and irreducible; the examiner could not get above the swelling. The clinical impression was a hydrocele, and he was scheduled for surgical repair. Initial triage investigations showed a hemoglobin level of 11.5 g/dL, blood group B Rh-positive, and microscopic examination of the urine and stool was normal, with no parasite ova detected.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The cystic, irreducible left scrotal mass was initially diagnosed as a routine hydrocele; however, surgical exploration revealed a thickened tunica albuginea and firm nodular lesions over the surface of an atrophic testis, with histology confirming chronic parasitic granulomatous inflammation.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient was planned for hydrocelectomy. Initial investigation showed hemoglobin of 11.5 gm/dL, blood group B Rh+, and urine and stool was normal with no ova. The patient underwent surgery; the findings were a hydrocele, thickened tunica and small nodules on the surface of the testis which created suspicion for testicular tumor, and orchidectomy was done.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Operative discovery of firm nodular lesions on the testicular surface raised high suspicion of a primary testicular tumor, prompting orchidectomy; however, histopathology revealed that the testis was uninvolved by neoplasm, exhibiting atrophic fibrosis alongside tunical granulomas surrounding parasite eggs.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The testis was not involved, and it showed atrophic changes with fibrosis; epididymis was also normal showing only dilatation.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Histopathological evaluation of the excised thickened tunica albuginea revealed active chronic granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid macrophages, foreign body giant cells, eosinophils, and numerous uncalcified eggs displaying a terminal spine characteristic of Schistosoma haematobium.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Histological examination with haematoxylin and eosin stain (H and E) showed active chronic granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid macrophages and foreign body giant cells and numerous schistosomal eggs in the thickened tunica albugenia with eosinophils infiltrate... Close examination of the eggs showed the terminal spine consistent with S. haematobium; the eggs was not calcified (see Figures 1, 2, and 3), indicating active inflammation.

editor_comments: Genital schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma haematobium mimicking hydrocele and testicular neoplasm, resulting in testicular atrophy in a 9-year-old Tanzanian boy.
